cards.title: Three-Level Outreach Personalization
cards.summary: Build outreach personalization in three layers: use their name, name their specific product, and add a detail that proves you consume their content.
cards.use_when: Writing ad-agency or freelance outreach DMs/emails to ecommerce store owners to win a copy or CRO engagement.
steps: Layer 1 — Personalize: replace 'to whom it may concern' with their first name and name their actual product instead of 'your product.'

Layer 2 — Detail: reference one concrete, specific thing that proves you've consumed their content — a video segment, an old post, or a detail from a recent story (e.g. 'I know you're probably busy with the launch you mentioned on your story').

Layer 3 — Proof of tenure: when possible, show objective evidence of long-term following (an inbox screenshot showing their emails dating back years, or a subscription date). The source treats this as unfakeable proof of genuine interest.
Keep the whole message short — the source notes prospects' inboxes are already full (he cites 5,000+ unread emails in his own) and long first messages simply don't get read.
caveats: The source says most outreach is generic and fails for exactly this reason — the bar is being different and better, not perfect.
Skip proofs of tenure you can't back up; faking a screenshot is the same sloppy-outreach failure mode.

cards.title: Instagram DM Ladder: Opener → Marinate → Value → Pitch
cards.summary: On Instagram, reply to a story or send a genuine compliment to earn a reply, wait, then offer value, deliver it, and only then pitch a call.
cards.use_when: Running Instagram DM outreach to ecommerce brand owners as a copywriter, media buyer or conversion consultant.
steps: Open with a story reply question or a genuine compliment/observation about something on their page — never a generic compliment like 'cool website colors.'
Objective of the opener is one reply, which moves you from the Request tab into Primary/General where they're notified of future messages. Don't pitch in the opener.
Marinate: do nothing. Complimenting and pitching in the same message reads as spammy — let the reply land, then wait a couple of days.
Offer value in curiosity language ('I made you this — want me to send it?') and make the offer easy to accept: don't ask them for data like open rates just to receive your free work.
Make your value easy to consume — a short loom, not a 20–30 minute video; the source emphasizes 'value per minute' over total minutes.
Pitch the call only after they've consumed the value — either inside the video or in the message that delivers it — framed as 'worth a quick call to see if this could work for you?'
caveats: Source: reply-to-story and compliment openers only work if you were genuinely following them and reply to real content; a compliment on a generic element gets ignored.
Bait-and-rizz / bait-and-switch is explicitly deprecated here: 'it doesn't really work that well' — offered value up front is the point.

cards.title: Curious Not Promising: Outreach on Business Owners
cards.summary: Frame outreach as curious possibility instead of big revenue promises, because sophisticated business owners read grandiose claims as dishonest.
cards.use_when: Writing the value/offer section of outreach to ecommerce founders and marketing leads.
steps: Replace promises ('I'll 10x your revenue') with curiosity-based hypotheses: 'I had some ideas that could possibly improve X — want to see?'
Use possibility hedges tied to outcomes store owners already care about (revenue, email revenue, ROAS on their ad spend, signups) rather than a forecast you can't support.
Ask what they want before deciding what to pitch. Source example: the specific lever could be more sales, more email signups, or lower ad costs — you don't know until you ask.
Use open-ended questions to invite them to describe their business and bottlenecks; the answers shape the actual proposal.
Anchor the whole exchange in 'mutual fit' qualification — you're qualifying them at the same time they qualify you, so the call is about fit, not a close.
Follow up from different angles with more free value; the source points out nobody can be angry at a follow-up that carries value.
caveats: Source explicitly says business owners are more skeptical and sophisticated than average consumers — big claims get written off as lies.
This is the source's stated approach, not a universal mandate; it also notes that outreach is 'a skills game,' so the value offered must actually be strong or it gets ignored.

cards.title: Universal Outreach Structure: Opener → Offer → Give → Pitch
cards.summary: Sequence outreach in four beats — attention-grabbing opener, value offer, delivery of that value, then the call pitch — with channel-specific compression.
cards.use_when: Designing any cold outreach sequence (DM, email) aimed at ecommerce brands.
steps: Beat 1 — Opener: grab attention with a question, curiosity, or a bold statement that references something specific about them; keep it brief.
Beat 2 — Offer value: 'I made this — want to see it?' Do not attach the actual deliverable before they opt in; a bad inbox owner may never consume it and you wasted the effort.
Beat 3 — Give value: deliver a high-quality, efficient-to-produce, easy-to-consume asset (short loom, a few sample emails, or annotated sales page).
Beat 4 — Pitch the call: either inside the video at the end or in the delivery message, framed around whether the value could work for them.
Compress for email: since email isn't a long back-and-forth chat like Instagram DMs, put opener AND value offer in the same first email, then follow up.

Find the actual email address for the person, not a general company address — the source recommends the apollo.io Chrome extension on a LinkedIn profile, but verify its current interface before relying on it.
caveats: The 'warmed-up' sending email matters: the source warns a brand-new address sending ~20/day lands in spam and recommends a warm-up service like Warmy for new domains.
A 72-hour client-getting result comes from testimonial examples, not a guarantee; results varied widely in the source's own examples.

cards.title: PDCW Opener Formula
cards.summary: Write cold openers with Personalize, Detailed, Curious, Witty — four traits that make a first message feel human and un-templated.
cards.use_when: Drafting the first line of an outreach DM or email to a store owner.
steps: Personalize — their name and their named product instead of generic greetings.
Detailed — one specific, checkable reference to their business (a video segment you watched, a promo they're currently running, a hobby they post about) that shows you did research.
Curious — say you have 'some tweaks to your funnel that could potentially increase profits' rather than listing the exact fix; the source says naming the fix removes curiosity and signals a template.
Witty — add a human, lightly humorous line so it doesn't read like software or an AI bot; the source argues the volume-spam approach produces 'dookie' results.
Length test: if your opener wouldn't make someone reply while standing in line, cut it down.
caveats: The source says curiosity has to be honest — vague lines still need to lead to real, specific value once they reply.
Wit is personality-dependent; heavy-handed jokes in a serious B2B store context may misfire.

cards.title: Prospect Outside Your Current Channel
cards.summary: Don't run outreach on one platform forever — master one channel for about a month, then layer a second to double channels and chances.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to expand outreach effort after establishing an initial channel.
steps: Pick one platform (Instagram, email, LinkedIn, YouTube, TikTok) and run outreach exclusively there for roughly a month until the motion is working.
After that period, start adding a second prospecting platform slowly — the source's logic is that doubling channels roughly doubles your shots at getting reply opportunities.

When identifying a prospect on TikTok/YouTube who runs a program (e.g. a 'content accelerator' or a 'training 100 people' announcement), the source classifies 'I'm planning to train 100 people' as a tell that they run a high-ticket offer — a signal they may value conversion help.
Outreach on Instagram or email even when you found them on YouTube or TikTok — the source recommends those two as the channels to actually message.
If the prospect's sales page looks self-written, note the exact weakness (unclear proof, weak offer framing) so your first value asset targets it.
caveats: This is the source's advice for service outreach; the store-side adaptation is that the same channel-expansion logic applies when a brand wants more acquisition channels, but the evidence here is about service client-getting.
TikTok/YouTube prospect channel recommendations may change with platform inbox and DM policies.

cards.title: Network Outreach in 72 Hours (Non-Direct Pitch)
cards.summary: Ask everyone you know — and their network — for referrals using a non-direct, no-pitch message that requests a discovery-project introduction.
cards.use_when: When starting freelance/agency outreach with no cold pipeline yet, or helping a store owner get their first affiliate/B2B intros through warm contacts.
steps: Step 1: spend ~30 minutes writing down everyone you know who owns a business or knows someone who owns a business — including weak ties you haven't considered.

Step 2: message each with a non-direct ask: explain you're starting out and looking for first case studies, and ask if they know anyone who'd be interested in free work or a small discovery project to test your skills.
Never pitch the contact directly ('can I work for you?') — the source emphasizes preserving the relationship by asking for a referral instead.
Step 3: when a referral replies, ask them what they need rather than pitching a pre-scripted offer; source says 'they have the answers you're looking for.'
Set a 72-hour timer after the video/instructions and run the method before judging it; the source gives examples of wins at 11 hours, second day, and fourth outreach.
caveats: Results in the source are student testimonials, not consistent performance; the source itself says 'not everybody's going to get clients this way.'
The source warns against memorizing scripts for the referral conversation — principles (like chess) beat memorized lines.

cards.title: The Give-Back Principle for Upfront Outreach Value
cards.summary: Give serious free value before asking for money — reciprocity, demonstrated skill, and differentiation drive more conversions than a pitch.
cards.use_when: Deciding what free asset to send a store owner before proposing paid copy/CRO work.
steps: Choose a free asset format that demonstrates copy skill directly on their business: sample emails for their welcome or abandoned-cart sequence, a short loom audit of their sales page or funnel, or a rewritten headline/hero section.
Make it genuinely high quality — the source argues the giveaway IS your free trial and your proof; weak free work gets ghosted, and that outcome signals your skill level.
Keep creation fast and consumption short: high value per minute, not long videos or 30-page documents.
Follow up with additional value from a different angle after the first giveaway rather than a nudge — 'nobody can get mad at you for following up with more free value.'
Use the reciprocity lever to convert: when someone receives concrete free work and it lands, the source's own experience was clients starting retainers (citing $3k/month) without a paid trial.
caveats: Documented outcomes are the presenter's own client experience, not a benchmark; the source's phrasing ('that's basically all the clients I've worked with') is anecdotal.
Free upfront work is uncompensated labor; scope it to one bounded, reusable asset so it doesn't become an unpaid full project.

cards.title: Cold Email: Warm the Sender, Combine Opener + Offer
cards.summary: Use a warmed sending address, put opener and value offer in the first email, then run a multi-angle follow-up sequence.
cards.use_when: Building a cold email play for ecommerce prospects when DMs aren't reaching decision makers.
steps: Scrape the decision maker's direct email — not a general company address — using the source's recommended route: find them on LinkedIn and use the apollo.io Chrome extension to reveal the address (verify current extension behavior and legality in your target market).

Use an email that has been used for real correspondence for a couple of years; a brand-new address sending ~20/day risks landing in spam per the source. If you need a new address, use a warm-up service to build deliverability over time.
In the first email, include both the opener and the value offer, since email doesn't have the back-and-forth rhythm of DMs.
Make the outside look important and the inside witty/personable and personal.
End with a strong, easy-to-say-yes value offer.
Deploy a follow-up sequence if no reply, rotating angles — the source calls follow-up 'almost just as if not more important' than the outreach itself.
caveats: Cold email deliverability rules change frequently; treat the warmed-address advice as directional and verify current provider guidance.
Apollo.io usage is subject to data-protection rules (GDPR/CAN-SPAM); confirm legality for your sending region.

cards.title: Follow-Up Is the Neglected Half of Outreach
cards.summary: Most people quit after one message; following up repeatedly from different angles with new value is where outreach actually converts.
cards.use_when: Reviving no-reply outreach threads and warm leads in a store's B2B or partner pipeline.
steps: Assume no reply means 'not yet seen,' not 'not interested' — the source blames most reported outreach failure on people stopping after one send.
Reach out again from a different angle: lead with a different problem, a different free artifact, or a new observation from their recent activity.
Attach fresh value rather than just a nudge ('more free value' follow-ups are the source's recommended pattern and are hard to resent).
Track which angle each prospect has seen so you never deliver the same artifact twice.
Build the sequence into the system, not your memory — the source describes follow-up as a structural stage of outreach, not a one-off action.
caveats: The source doesn't give cadence numbers to copy; rather than invent a schedule, keep the angle-diversity rule and stop if asked to.
Repeated contact without new value is the failure mode the source attributes to most 'I tried outreach and it didn't work' stories.

cards.title: Why Free Work Isn't Risk-Free for the Brand
cards.summary: Prospective clients hesitate because bad copy damages brand, leads and reputation — free doesn't remove that risk, so prove competence up front.
cards.use_when: Framing your offer to a store owner who is gun-shy about handing over their email or PDP copy.
steps: Acknowledge the real risk from the brand's side: bad copy can harm messaging, leads and reputation even if the copywriter is unpaid — the source states this can cost six figures.
Counter the risk with demonstrated brand-voice matching: consume their content (posts, videos, newsletter), then write the free artifact in their voice.
Reference their newsletter content or old posts in outreach to show you understand their brand's stance — 'so they don't have to babysit you.'
Show speed and initiative: deliver a tight piece of work that proves you can operate without heavy oversight.
On the call, use 'mutual fit' framing and small-project-first language to keep the risk low for both sides.
caveats: The six-figure damage figure is the source's illustrative claim, not a measured benchmark.
Matching a brand's voice on one asset doesn't guarantee you can carry a full account; be honest about scope.

cards.title: Two Outreach Failure Modes: Post-and-Pray and Volume Spam
cards.summary: Avoid the two archetypes that never work: lowballing passively and blasting generic high-volume messages that scream desperation.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your outreach strategy before scaling it, especially on Upwork or DMs.
steps: Failure mode 1 — post-and-pray: create a profile, announce you're an eager copywriter, set rates very low, and wait. The source says nothing happens and people conclude copywriting 'didn't work.'

Failure mode 2 — volume spam: use software tricks to send 100–300 identical messages per day ('I'm a copywriter, I can make you more money, book a call'). The source says no one pays $2k–$4k/month for that.
Replace both with personalization volume: fewer, researched, specific messages that make the recipient feel like the only one you're talking to.
Use proof of work rather than volume claims — no one responds to 'I send 1000 outreaches a day' as evidence of quality.
When scaling, scale verified specifics (data, angles, testable hooks), never copy-paste reach.
caveats: Volume isn't inherently wrong — the source's objection is generic, non-personalized volume. High-volume personalized systems can still work if personalization is real.
Low-price positioning is framed as a trap in this source; this is the presenter's opinion about client acquisition, not a universal pricing law.

cards.title: Value-Offer Sizing: Easy to Accept, Easy to Consume
cards.summary: Make the value offer trivial to say yes to and the delivered asset fast to consume — the source prioritizes value per minute.
cards.use_when: Designing the free audit, loom, or sample-work offer a store owner receives before a paid engagement.
steps: Word the offer as if the work already exists: 'I had spare time today and recorded a loom showing X — want me to send it over?' instead of asking for access or data first.
Never make acceptance require work from them — no 'send me your open rates' or 'fill out this form' before they can receive the value.
Cap the asset length: short loom or a handful of sample emails; long documents and 20–30 minute videos lose the viewer part-way through.
Optimize value per minute, not total minutes delivered — the source is explicit that dense short assets beat long diluted ones.
Follow the delivery with the call pitch, framed as checking whether the value could work for them.
caveats: The source's phrasing about making the value sound 'already created' is a delivery convention, not a permission to mislead — actually create it before promising to send.
No hard length thresholds are given; the 20–30 minute video comment is the presenter's viewing-behavior observation.

cards.title: Give Value From Curiosity, Not a Promise of Revenue
cards.summary: If your opener says 'I'll double your revenue,' you've made it about a promise; if it asks whether a specific improvement could help, it's a conversation.
cards.use_when: Writing the value/benefit language in the first DM or cold email to a store owner or marketing lead.
steps: State what you observed and what could change, not what will definitely happen — e.g. 'I noticed your Nurture sequence could potentially increase revenue' beats 'this will make you $50k.'
Ask at least one open question in the message; the source says this both reduces resistance and reveals what the client actually cares about.
Avoid asking for their data before the value offer — curiosity should not become homework.
When a prospect replies with interest, re-frame what you'll build around their answer, not a preloaded promise.
Follow up with more value from another angle if they don't reply; don't escalate the promise in the follow-up.
caveats: Curiosity framing can read as evasive if you never become specific once they respond; the payoff of the curiosity frame is what you reveal next.
This is the source's stated philosophy for business owners specifically, whom it describes as highly sales-literate.

cards.title: Turn Free Value Into Paid Work by Shipping the Value First
cards.summary: Deliver one concrete piece of value (an email sequence, a loom audit) so the client experiences your skill before any sales conversation, then quote the retainer.
cards.use_when: Converting a warm cold-outreach prospect into a paid email/SMS or CRO engagement.
steps: Pick a bounded, high-leverage deliverable the store actually needs — the source's example: write improved emails for a promotion they're running, or annotate their sales page.
Send the value free — no contract, no trial agreement, just the work — so the owner experiences the output directly.
After they respond positively, pitch the paid engagement; the source's pattern for a fit result was a retainer starting around $3k/month without a paid trial.
Keep the ask about fit: 'let's work together on a small project to see if we'd be a good fit.'
If they ghost after receiving the value, treat it as a signal the free value wasn't strong enough (source's read), and make the next one better.
caveats: The $3k/month retainer figure is the presenter's own experience and should not be presented to store owners as a benchmark for their situation.
Bounded free work can be copied without payment; pick a deliverable that's clearly part of a larger system.

cards.title: Only Offer Value After They've Replied
cards.summary: Hold off creating the free asset until the prospect has opted in, so you don't build value for people who never see it.
cards.use_when: Sequencing the outreach flow so time isn't spent creating assets for non-responsive prospects.
steps: Send the opener first on DM channels; the goal is one reply and no deliverable.
After the reply, send the value offer as a description, not the asset itself — 'I made you this, want me to send it?'
Only create/deliver the asset once they say yes. The source's rationale: they may not check DMs, an assistant may check them, or they may never look, wasting your time.
On email, compress and include opener + value offer in the first email because email is asynchronous and leaner.
Keep the offered artifact scoped so creating it fast is realistic once they say yes.
caveats: Delaying delivery can feel withholding if your offer is vague; the offer must be concrete enough to be worth saying yes to.
If you overpromise the content of the asset, you lose credibility when it arrives.

cards.title: Subject-Line Style Intrigue for DMs
cards.summary: Instagram shows a preview of your first words; make them intriguing enough to earn the open and don't stack multiple messages.
cards.use_when: Writing the first line of an Instagram DM pitch to an ecommerce founder.
steps: Treat the first line of a DM like an email subject line — it's the only thing visible in the inbox preview.

The source's judgment on examples: '4 messages' (multiple stacked messages) is least likely to be opened, 'yo [name] can you let me know something' reads like a request for value and is weak, 'view photo' is intriguing, and a contextual opener like 'I know you're probably busy [doing their specific thing]' performs well.
Drop greetings like 'hi [name]' when space is tight; get into the intrigue immediately.
Localize the opener to their life or business: source example, for a trainer who always touts leg press over squats, reference that inside joke rather than a generic 'I know you're busy.'
Don't send a follow-up message immediately after a story reply — the preview then shows 'N messages' and kills the open rate.
caveats: Open rate behavior in the source is the presenter's own inbox experience, not measured data.
Instagram's preview treatment may change; verify the current interface if this is central to your play.

cards.title: Find Prospect Emails With Apollo.io
cards.summary: Use the Apollo.io Chrome extension on a prospect's LinkedIn profile to reveal a direct email when their other channels don't expose one.
cards.use_when: Sourcing decision-maker email addresses for cold email outreach to ecommerce brands.
steps: Install the Apollo.io Chrome extension from the browser store.
Open the prospect's LinkedIn profile (the source uses LinkedIn as the lookup point).
The extension pops up in the corner; use it to view the revealed email address.
Cross-check the address type — the source insists on reaching the person, not a general company inbox, so prefer direct addresses tied to the individual.
Pair the found email with a warmed sending address before you begin volume outreach.
caveats: The extension's current behavior, plan limits and legality vary by region; verify the current interface and your data-protection obligations.
The source explicitly discourages sending from a brand-new email address, so source the address and the warmed sender together.

cards.title: Outreach Is a Skills Game, Not a Numbers Game
cards.summary: Your results track the quality of the free value you produce, not the volume of messages sent — so build the underlying skill before scaling outreach.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to scale outreach volume or improve the quality of the copy/offer you send.
steps: Before increasing volume, test whether your current value offer is actually strong: the source treats being ghosted after free value delivery as evidence the value wasn't good enough.
Invest in marketing/copy skill because it directly determines the quality of the free asset (sample emails, sales page critiques, looms).
When you do get a client, treat it as compounding skill evidence: first paid work gives you proof and confidence, not just cash.
Use one bounded paid project (source example: $100 for a small email batch) as a foot-in-the-door to build social proof and counter impostor syndrome, then reprice.
Keep improving personalization and angle diversity rather than copying templates verbatim — source argues copied scripts have usually already been seen by the prospect.
caveats: The source's own framing is that this is his philosophy and experience; it does not deny that volume plays a role — it argues quality governs results.
The $100 starter project is presented as a source example of a first step, not a recommended market rate.
